h1:
Nong Khai 2 Days 1 Night
Mekong, Sala Kaew Ku & Tha Sadet Market
intro: Nong Khai is a town to visit without rushing. It's small, so a car or a rented motorbike gets you around the whole place easily. The draw is the Mekong River running right through the center: cool evening breezes and the sun setting over the Laos side make for a scene people come back for. This plan covers two days and one night — the riverfront, the strange and striking Sala Kaew Ku, the long walkable Tha Sadet Market, and the spots locals actually go to.
chips: 🌊 Riverside walks in the cool breeze

blocks.html: First, a quick lay of the land. Nong Khai sits right on the Laos border, only about 55 km from Udon Thani. Many people fly into Udon and drive an hour to reach Nong Khai. The town itself is compact, and the main sights line up along the Mekong, close enough to walk between several of them. Sala Kaew Ku and Wat Pha Tak Suea are a little outside town, so having a vehicle makes things smoother. This plan keeps day one to the riverfront in town, then heads out of town on day two for Sala Kaew Ku and a temple visit before you leave.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Into town, the Mekong, and Tha Sadet Market

items.activity: Arrive in Nong Khai, check in at a place in town
items.note: Pick somewhere near the riverfront or close to Tha Sadet Market so you can wander on foot at night without driving.

items.activity: Lunch at the Vietnamese spot, Daeng Naem Nuang
items.note: A long-running, well-known Vietnamese restaurant in town. The nem nuang is charcoal-grilled and made fresh daily; add the sugarcane shrimp and fried spring rolls.

items.activity: Pay respects to Luang Pho Phra Sai at Wat Pho Chai
items.note: A roughly 300-year-old temple at the heart of town life. Luang Pho Phra Sai is a revered Buddha image honored by both Thai and Lao people, so dress modestly.

items.activity: Coffee break at a riverside cafe or old-town building
items.note: There are cafes in colonial-style buildings close to a century old, with a feel a bit like Luang Prabang. Good for sipping coffee out of the afternoon sun before heading to the river.

items.activity: Stroll the Naga Plaza by the Mekong
items.note: The town landmark — the pair of Naga statues in front of Wat Lamduan, next to Tha Sadet Market. Locals come here in the evening to walk, cycle, and exercise.

items.activity: Watch the sunset over the Laos side
items.note: The golden hour over the Mekong is the highlight of the day. Find a seat on the riverbank or at a waterside spot, order something, and wait for the evening light.

items.activity: Eat your way through Tha Sadet Market
items.note: An old riverside market with plenty of snacks. Try the pate bread (French bread filled with liver pâté and Vietnamese pork sausage) and pick up dried goods and souvenirs from Laos.
Pick a place doing Mekong river fish or an Isan spot by the water. End the day with the cool breeze, then walk back to your room.

blocks.title: About Tha Sadet Market hours
blocks.html: Tha Sadet Market has both a morning zone and an evening zone, and the hours listed by different sources don't quite line up. Broadly, the food and souvenir section runs from around 8:00 until evening, while the morning market starts as early as 5 a.m. If you want it at its liveliest, evening to early night is the sweet spot.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Sala Kaew Ku, the submerged stupa, and skywalk views

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Out of town and temple visits

items.activity: Breakfast at your hotel or a morning spot in town
items.note: Nong Khai has plenty of breakfast options — rice porridge, old-style coffee, bread with kaya. Take your pick before setting off.
A sculpture park on about 42 rai (roughly 7 hectares), around 3 km from town, with over 200 giant cement sculptures. The angles here are unlike anywhere else and fun to photograph.

items.activity: Stop at the submerged stupa (Phra That La Nong)
items.note: An old stupa that collapsed and sits in the middle of the Mekong. When the water drops you can see its base clearly — a pretty, peaceful river viewpoint.

items.activity: Lunch before heading out of town
items.note: Refuel at midday. If you're continuing to Wat Pha Tak Suea, eat well, since the distance gets longer from here.

items.activity: Walk the Wat Pha Tak Suea skywalk (optional)
items.note: A glass-floored skywalk with high-up views of the Mekong, out of town toward Sangkhom. You'll want your own vehicle; if time is tight, skip ahead to the next stop.

items.activity: Photo stop at the 1st Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge
items.note: The bridge runs over 1,170 m, linking Nong Khai with Vientiane. A nice riverside photo spot, both by day and in the evening.
Grab souvenirs around Tha Sadet Market or shops in town — mu yo, naem, Chinese sausage — before catching a ride back to Udon or the train.

blocks.title: Sala Kaew Ku entry fee
blocks.html: Entry is around 20 THB for Thai adults, 10 THB for children, and roughly 40 THB for foreigners, open about 8:00–18:00. The midday sun is fairly strong since you're walking outdoors the whole time, so morning or late afternoon is best. Bring a hat and water.

blocks.text: Nong Khai food worth trying on this trip

blocks.html: Nong Khai is a border town that blends Isan culture with Vietnamese and Lao influences, so the food comes in many styles all within walking distance. Here are the dishes and spots locals actually go to, in the order I'd suggest trying them on a short trip.

items.name: Nem nuang — Daeng Naem Nuang
items.blurb: The town's famous spot. The nem nuang is made fresh daily, skewered and grilled over charcoal the old-fashioned way, wrapped with rice paper and fresh herbs and dipped in the house sauce. Most people who come to Nong Khai stop here.

items.name: Mekong river fish — riverside restaurants
items.blurb: A Mekong town calls for freshwater fish — as tom yum, fish larb, or fried with chili sauce. The fish is fresh from the river, and it goes especially well with a river view at dusk.

items.name: Pate bread (French bread) — Tha Sadet Market
items.blurb: Bread that's crisp outside and soft inside, filled with liver pâté and Vietnamese pork sausage — a Vietnamese influence. An easy snack to eat while you walk the market.

items.name: Sugarcane shrimp
items.blurb: Minced shrimp wrapped around a stick of sugarcane and grilled, with a faint sweet aroma. Usually ordered alongside the nem nuang at Vietnamese restaurants.

items.name: Fried spring rolls
items.blurb: Generously filled spring rolls fried until crisp, dipped in sweet-and-sour sauce. A popular snack at Nong Khai's Vietnamese restaurants.

items.name: Riverside Isan food
items.blurb: Som tam, larb, koi, grilled pork neck — all the bold flavors, found at the riverside restaurants and eaten with cold sticky rice.

items.name: Coffee in an old-town building
items.blurb: A cafe in a colonial building close to a century old, with a Luang Prabang feel. A good place to rest out of the afternoon sun between sights.

items.name: Nong Khai-style breakfast
items.blurb: Rice noodle porridge, old-style coffee, bread with kaya — a border-town breakfast that's easy to find all over town.

items.name: Mu yo and naem — Nong Khai souvenirs
items.blurb: The souvenirs to carry home — firm-textured mu yo and naem with just the right tang. Find them at Tha Sadet Market and shops in town.

blocks.text: The main sights in this plan

items.name: Naga Plaza by the Mekong
items.blurb: The landmark pair of Naga statues in front of Wat Lamduan, next to Tha Sadet Market. Stroll for the cool breeze and the sunset.

items.name: Tha Sadet Market
items.blurb: An old riverside market packed with food and souvenirs, open morning to evening, liveliest at dusk.

items.name: Sala Kaew Ku (Wat Khaek)
items.blurb: A sculpture park with over 200 cement figures on about 42 rai, full of offbeat angles, around 3 km from town.

items.name: Wat Pho Chai (Luang Pho Phra Sai)
items.blurb: A roughly 300-year-old town temple housing Luang Pho Phra Sai, a sacred image revered on both banks of the Mekong.

items.name: 1st Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge
items.blurb: A Mekong crossing over 1,170 m long, linking Nong Khai with Vientiane — a popular riverside photo spot.

items.name: Wat Pha Tak Suea (skywalk)
items.blurb: A glass-floored skywalk with high-up Mekong views, a bit far out of town — an optional add-on if you have a car and time.

blocks.text: How to get there and get around smoothly

items: From Bangkok — fly into Udon Thani then drive about 1 hour to Nong Khai, or take a train/coach straight to Nong Khai station.
In town — the riverfront, Tha Sadet Market, and Naga Plaza are close together and walkable; no vehicle needed.
Out of town — Sala Kaew Ku, the Friendship Bridge, and Wat Pha Tak Suea are smoother with your own vehicle or a rented motorbike than waiting for public transport.
Crossing to Vientiane — with an extra day, cross at the Friendship Bridge to visit the Laos side. Have your passport ready.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Nong Khai is a quiet, slow-paced town — it doesn't have sights packed in like a big city. The charm is the riverside atmosphere and getting to take it slow. If you come looking for a buzz you might be let down, but if you want to sit and watch the river, eat well, and visit temples, this town hits the mark.

items: 1 night's stay — hotels/guesthouses in the riverside part of town start at around ฿500–1,200 per night.
Food — main meals at riverside/Vietnamese spots run about ฿150–300 each, plus market snacks.
Entry fees — Sala Kaew Ku ฿20; most everything else is free (temples, Naga Plaza, the market).
Getting around locally — a motorbike rents for around ฿200–300 per day, or use your own vehicle / local rides in town.
Total per person — for a relaxed, not-extravagant trip, about ฿1,500–2,500 per person (not counting travel into the province).

faq.q: What can you see in Nong Khai in 2 days and 1 night?
faq.a: Day one focuses on the riverfront in town: pay respects to Luang Pho Phra Sai at Wat Pho Chai, walk Naga Plaza, catch the sunset, then eat your way through Tha Sadet Market. Day two heads out of town to Sala Kaew Ku, with stops at the submerged stupa and the Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge. With a car and extra time you can add the Wat Pha Tak Suea skywalk.

faq.q: How much is entry to Sala Kaew Ku, and what are the hours?
faq.a: Entry is around 20 THB for Thai adults, 10 THB for children, and roughly 40 THB for foreigners, open about 8:00–18:00. It's around 3 km from town, and you walk through the outdoor sculptures, so bring a hat and water as the midday sun is fairly strong.

faq.q: What time does Tha Sadet Market open, and what's there to eat?
faq.a: Broadly, the food and souvenir section runs from around 8:00 until evening, while the morning market starts as early as 5 a.m. Highlights are the pate bread, snacks, and souvenirs like mu yo, naem, and Chinese sausage, plus goods from Laos. It's liveliest from evening into early night.

faq.q: What's the easiest way to get to Nong Khai?
faq.a: The popular route is to fly into Udon Thani then drive about 1 hour to Nong Khai, or take a train/coach straight to Nong Khai. In town the riverfront sights are walkable, while Sala Kaew Ku and Wat Pha Tak Suea are out of town, so you'll want a car or a rented motorbike.

faq.q: What Nong Khai food should you try?
faq.a: First up is nem nuang at a famous Vietnamese spot like Daeng Naem Nuang, then Mekong river fish at the riverside restaurants, pate bread at Tha Sadet Market, sugarcane shrimp, fried spring rolls, and souvenirs like mu yo and naem.
